issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' is an avoidance/safety behaviour rather than a threat appraisal item. In this profile, the Threat node otherwise contains felt current danger and reliving; this item is misclassified and weakens within-node coherence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is not phrased as a strategy and appears to describe a trigger category. It is also weakly supported by the rest of the profile, since no memory, threat, or appraisal content specifically involves authorities or uniforms. This creates a cross-node mismatch and a node-level inconsistency within Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Nadia is a 55-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who now works as an HVAC technician, a job that keeps her moving through apartment basements, rooftops, utility rooms, and tight mechanical spaces across the city. She is divorced and lives alone. When she began describing why she had come for help, she started not with the present but with the period when she fled her home country as a refugee, speaking in a halting way that made clear how difficult it was for her to stay with the memory for long. There had been a crossing in which water was everywhere-too much of it, dark and uncontrolled-and the conditions around her were chaotic enough that even now she struggles to tell the story in a way that feels real to her. She said that when she thinks about that time, part of her still cannot believe it happened to her, as if she is recounting something that belongs to somebody else's life. Yet certain sensory details remain fixed: the sight of rising water, the feel of a particular wet, rough material against her hands and clothes, the bodily knowledge that there was no safe way to predict what would happen next.

In telling it, Nadia becomes visibly strained. She has to stop and gather herself because when the memory comes back it does not come back as a distant narrative. It returns with a force that leaves her flooded by feeling, unable to continue speaking, and ashamed in a way she finds hard to explain. She lowers her eyes and says she should have known more, done more, understood whom to trust. Just as often, she turns outward and circles around what others did to her and failed to do for her, replaying their decisions and betrayals again and again. She can spend hours dwelling on the people who put her in danger, those who made promises, those who looked away. The thoughts do not settle into conclusion; they loop.

Over the years since resettlement, the past has not stayed in the past in any simple way. In her work as an HVAC technician, she may enter a building for a routine call and immediately note every exit before she sets down her tools. She does this automatically now: front door, service corridor, stairwell, windows large enough to climb through if necessary. If she is sent to inspect a basement unit in an older building and sees pooled water near a drain, or hears that a lower level has flooded, her whole body tightens before she can think. Large decorative fountains in office lobbies, retention ponds beside commercial properties, even a stretch of standing water in a mechanical room can affect her more than she wants to admit. There are moments when she suddenly feels as though she is back there again, not remembering but reliving. In those moments she may freeze, grip her equipment, or orient herself as if immediate escape is required.

Texture is another trigger she did not understand for a long time. Certain damp, coarse materials-insulation, old woven utility fabric, saturated carpeting-can provoke an immediate recoil. She notices the sensation in her hands first, then a rush of dread. She has become skilled at hiding this on the job, stepping away under the pretense of checking a valve or retrieving another tool. Colleagues know her as meticulous and unusually alert. They do not always see how much energy goes into constantly scanning every room, every stairwell, every sound shift around her. What unsettles her most is silence. If a building goes suddenly quiet-the hum of equipment cuts out, voices disappear, a hallway falls still-she feels certain that danger is close. Silence does not register as calm to her; it feels like a warning.

Uncertainty is particularly hard for Nadia to bear. Last-minute schedule changes from dispatch, unclear access instructions from property managers, delays while she waits alone for someone to unlock a service area-these moments can stir intense agitation. She wants to know exactly where she is going, who will be there, how she will leave. Over time this has narrowed her life. She avoids outings if she cannot picture the layout in advance. She chooses seats near doors, arrives early so she can study a space, and leaves places abruptly if she cannot identify a clear exit. In relationships this has made her seem distant and guarded. After her divorce, she became even more self-reliant, telling herself that depending on others is dangerous because people can trap you, fail you, or hand your fate to chance.

By the time Nadia sought treatment, she was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of threat. What finally pushed her to come in was an incident at work after a flooded utility room call, when the combination of standing water, wet flooring under her boots, and a sudden silence after the power was cut left her feeling as if the refugee crossing were happening again. She had to leave the site and sit in her van until she could breathe steadily. She was shaken not only by the intensity of the episode but by the realization that her world had become organized around anticipation and escape. She says she wants help because she is tired of living as if catastrophe is waiting behind every closed door. At the same time, she is frightened that if she lets her guard down even a little, she will be caught unprepared and overwhelmed all over again.
